changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For operations buyers at event-driven merchants, lead with 'A name, not a queue.' Introduce the named people on the account (solutions engineer and account lead), have them in the room, and put their names in the proposal. Then say who covers their biggest days. Only promise on-call cover for peak events if we can actually staff it. Do not open with tiers or response times when the buyer asks who.
changes.why: When Halima asked 'who's my person' she was walked through the support plans, which is essentially M5. She dismissed it as 'a queue with a faster timer'. The competitor won by putting named people in the room.

changes.change: Add a peak-event proof asset for event-driven merchants: a written plan for their on-sale morning, built with the solutions engineer before the decision meeting. It should state who is watching, who they call, and what happens at minute four. Suggested line: 'I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.' Here is exactly what happens on your on-sale morning.
changes.why: The decider explicitly asked to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning. The rep said we have no such asset and that he could have built one with our SE.

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For operations buyers, replace logo-led proof with a reference customer who can name the person who picked up when something went wrong on their biggest day. Offer it as a call, not a case study.
changes.why: The rep says 'I had logos. I didn't have a person.' The customer's pain was a provider whose support never picked up, so logos did not answer the decider's question.

changes.change: For event-driven merchants, open on incident ownership ahead of M1's global-growth line. Ask what happened the last time payments failed during a live sale, and who answered. Treat sandbox and load-test proof as the price of entry for the operations buyer, and keep it in the technical track with the CTO.
changes.why: The evaluation was triggered by an unanswered ticket form during a public on-sale failure, not by throughput. The decider met the load-test results with a single 'good.'
